---
title: "Benchmarks: R8, R52, MR, Ohsumed, 20NG"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r values, include = FALSE}
results <- read.csv("benchmark-results.csv")
published <- read.csv("benchmark-published.csv")
lowlabel <- read.csv("benchmark-lowlabel.csv")
unsupervised_effects <- read.csv("benchmark-umap-hdbscan-effects.csv")
bertopic_seeds <- read.csv("benchmark-bertopic-seeds.csv")
bertopic_effects <- read.csv("benchmark-bertopic-effects.csv")

result_of <- function(data, m, column = "accuracy") {
  subset(results, dataset == data & method == m)[[column]]
}
fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.4f", x)
pub <- function(data, m) fmt(subset(published, dataset == data & model == m)$accuracy)
low_at <- function(data, frac, m) {
  rows <- lowlabel[lowlabel$dataset == data & lowlabel$method == m, ]
  rows[abs(rows$fraction - frac) < 1e-9, ]
}
effect <- function(data, comp, metric, ref = NULL) {
  rows <- data[data$comparator == comp & data$metric == metric, ]
  if (!is.null(ref)) rows <- rows[rows$reference == ref, ]
  rows
}
largest <- subset(results, dataset == "20ng" & method == "hypergraph_zhou_cmn")
```

Label spreading on a hypergraph (Zhou et al. 2006) classifies documents in
closed form, without trained parameters. This article reports its test-set
accuracy on five standard text-classification benchmarks, R8, R52, MR,
Ohsumed and 20-Newsgroups, against a tf-idf nearest-centroid baseline and
the published accuracies of Ding et al. (2020). Every number not taken from
a publication was computed with the package on these corpora.

## Setup

The corpora and their training and test splits are the files of Yao, Mao and
Luo (2019), which Ding et al. (2020) also use. Each dataset becomes a sparse
document-word hypergraph with documents as nodes, words as hyperedges and
tf-idf incidence weights. The training documents are the labelled seeds, and
the spreading solution classifies every test document with one
conjugate-gradient solve per class.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
hg <- text_hypergraph(docs, weight = "tfidf", sparse = TRUE)
fit <- hg_classify(hg, labels = train_labels, normalization = "class_mass")
```

The split sizes match Table 1 of Ding et al. on all five datasets. The
vocabulary sizes match on R8 (`r format(result_of("R8", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn", "n_edges"), big.mark = ",")` hyperedges)
and R52 (`r format(result_of("R52", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn", "n_edges"), big.mark = ",")`).
On MR, Ohsumed and 20NG the vocabularies are smaller than the published ones
(`r format(result_of("mr", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn", "n_edges"), big.mark = ",")` against 18,764,
`r format(result_of("ohsumed", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn", "n_edges"), big.mark = ",")` against 14,157 and
`r format(result_of("20ng", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn", "n_edges"), big.mark = ",")` against 42,757), because
the tokenizer drops tokens that contain digits. One MR document is
unreachable from the rest of the corpus. It is in the training set, so no
test document is affected.

## Full-split results

`accuracy` is the test-set accuracy with a 1,000-resample percentile
bootstrap interval, and `fit_s` is the time in seconds of the transductive
solve.

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  subset(results,
         select = c(dataset, method, accuracy, ci_low, ci_high, macro_f1,
                    build_s, fit_s)),
  digits = 4
)
```

On the two datasets with balanced classes, label spreading is more accurate
than the centroid baseline: `r fmt(result_of("20ng", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))`
against `r fmt(result_of("20ng", "tfidf_centroid"))` on 20NG and
`r fmt(result_of("mr", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))` against
`r fmt(result_of("mr", "tfidf_centroid"))` on MR. On R8, R52 and Ohsumed,
whose classes are unbalanced, the centroid is more accurate. The largest
difference is on R52, with 52 unbalanced classes
(`r fmt(result_of("R52", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))` against
`r fmt(result_of("R52", "tfidf_centroid"))`).

The rows `hypergraph_zhou` use the argmax of Zhou et al. (2006) without
normalization. They assign most documents to the largest class: on R8 the
accuracy is `r fmt(result_of("R8", "hypergraph_zhou"))`, the share of the
largest class, and on 20NG it is `r fmt(result_of("20ng", "hypergraph_zhou"))`.
The class-mass normalization of Zhu, Ghahramani and Lafferty (2003) corrects
this and is used in every other row. Among the hypergraph methods, the random
walk with edge-dependent vertex weights (Chitra and Raphael 2019; Hayashi et
al. 2020), `hypergraph_random_walk_cmn`, is the most accurate on Ohsumed
(`r fmt(result_of("ohsumed", "hypergraph_random_walk_cmn"))` against
`r fmt(result_of("ohsumed", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))`).

The largest solve, 20NG with
`r format(largest$n_nodes, big.mark = ",")` documents,
`r format(largest$n_edges, big.mark = ",")` hyperedges and 20 classes,
takes `r sprintf("%.1f", largest$fit_s)` seconds on a laptop CPU. Table 3 of
Ding et al. reports 1,479 MB of GPU memory for TextGCN and 180 MB for
HyperGAT on the same corpus.

## Comparison with published results

The published rows are means over 10 runs from Table 2 of Ding et al.
(2020). The rows computed here are deterministic for a given split.

```{r}
knitr::kable(published, digits = 4)
```

On 20NG, label spreading (`r fmt(result_of("20ng", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))`)
is within two points of transductive TextGCN (`r pub("20ng", "TextGCN (transductive)")`)
and HyperGAT (`r pub("20ng", "HyperGAT")`) and above fastText
(`r pub("20ng", "fastText")`). On MR (`r fmt(result_of("mr", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))`)
it is close to transductive TextGCN (`r pub("mr", "TextGCN (transductive)")`)
and below HyperGAT (`r pub("mr", "HyperGAT")`). On R8, R52 and Ohsumed the
trained models are more accurate. A closed-form spectral method reaches
most of the accuracy of trained graph neural networks on corpora with
balanced classes and falls well short of it on corpora with unbalanced
classes.

## Few labels

Label spreading is designed for few labels. In this experiment the training
seeds are subsampled, stratified by class with at least one seed per class
and five draws per fraction, and both methods receive the same seeds. The
`sd` column is the standard deviation over the draws.

```{r}
knitr::kable(lowlabel, digits = 4)
```

On MR, label spreading is more accurate at every fraction, from
`r low_at("mr", 0.01, "hypergraph_zhou_cmn")$n_seeds` seeds
(`r fmt(low_at("mr", 0.01, "hypergraph_zhou_cmn")$accuracy)` against
`r fmt(low_at("mr", 0.01, "tfidf_centroid")$accuracy)`) to
`r format(low_at("mr", 0.2, "hypergraph_zhou_cmn")$n_seeds, big.mark = ",")`
seeds (`r fmt(low_at("mr", 0.2, "hypergraph_zhou_cmn")$accuracy)` against
`r fmt(low_at("mr", 0.2, "tfidf_centroid")$accuracy)`). On R8 and Ohsumed
the centroid is more accurate at every fraction. With unbalanced classes,
the tf-idf profile of each class survives the subsampling better than the
spreading solution does.

## Unsupervised clustering against UMAP and HDBSCAN

Clustering is compared on R8 without labels. `hg_cluster()` with eight
clusters is compared with TF-IDF/SVD embeddings reduced by UMAP (McInnes,
Healy and Melville 2018) and clustered either by HDBSCAN (Campello, Moulavi
and Sander 2013) or by k-means with eight clusters. This experiment does not
run the BERTopic package, which the next section does.

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  subset(unsupervised_effects,
         select = c(comparator, metric, hypergraphs_mean, baseline_mean,
                    mean_difference, difference_ci_low,
                    difference_ci_high, paired_dz)),
  digits = 4
)
```

HDBSCAN with its default settings divides R8 into many more than eight
clusters and leaves part of the corpus as outliers, so `hg_cluster()` agrees
more with the labels on all three measures. Against k-means with eight
clusters, `hg_cluster()` has the higher adjusted Rand index, by
`r fmt(effect(unsupervised_effects, "umap_kmeans_k8", "ari")$mean_difference)`
(95% paired bootstrap interval
`r fmt(effect(unsupervised_effects, "umap_kmeans_k8", "ari")$difference_ci_low)` to
`r fmt(effect(unsupervised_effects, "umap_kmeans_k8", "ari")$difference_ci_high)`),
and the lower adjusted mutual information and normalized mutual
information, by
`r fmt(-effect(unsupervised_effects, "umap_kmeans_k8", "ami")$mean_difference)`.

## BERTopic

The same R8 experiment was run with `bertopic.BERTopic` 0.17.4 (Grootendorst
2022) at its defaults: `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` sentence embeddings, UMAP with ten
seeds, HDBSCAN and c-TF-IDF. Three BERTopic variants are scored: the package
as shipped, where HDBSCAN chooses the number of topics and marks outliers;
the fitted model reduced to eight topics with `reduce_topics()`; and that
model with `reduce_outliers(strategy = "embeddings")`, which assigns every
document. Two hypergraph variants cluster into eight clusters with
`hg_cluster()`: the tf-idf document-word hypergraph, and a nearest-neighbour
hypergraph (`text_hypergraph(construction = "knn")`) built on the same
MiniLM vectors, which holds the embedding fixed and changes only the
clustering.

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  aggregate(cbind(ari, ami, nmi, n_clusters, outlier_fraction) ~ method,
            data = bertopic_seeds, FUN = mean),
  digits = 4, caption = "Means over ten seeds"
)
knitr::kable(
  subset(bertopic_effects, comparator == "bertopic_k_assigned",
         select = c(reference, metric, hypergraphs_mean, baseline_mean,
                    mean_difference, difference_ci_low,
                    difference_ci_high)),
  digits = 4, caption = "Paired effects against the fully assigned eight-topic BERTopic"
)
```

```{r bertopic-values, include = FALSE}
shipped <- subset(bertopic_seeds, method == "bertopic_default")
tfidf_ari <- effect(bertopic_effects, "bertopic_k_assigned", "ari",
                    "hypergraphs_hypergraph")
knn_ari <- effect(bertopic_effects, "bertopic_k_assigned", "ari",
                  "hypergraphs_knn_sbert")
knn_ami <- effect(bertopic_effects, "bertopic_k_assigned", "ami",
                  "hypergraphs_knn_sbert")
```

BERTopic as shipped finds `r min(shipped$n_clusters)` to
`r max(shipped$n_clusters)` topics and leaves
`r round(100 * mean(shipped$outlier_fraction))`% of R8 as outliers, so it
agrees least with the labels on every measure. Against the eight-topic
BERTopic that assigns every document, the tf-idf hypergraph has the higher
adjusted Rand index, by `r fmt(tfidf_ari$mean_difference)` (95% paired
bootstrap interval `r fmt(tfidf_ari$difference_ci_low)` to
`r fmt(tfidf_ari$difference_ci_high)`), and the nearest-neighbour hypergraph
on the same embeddings by `r fmt(knn_ari$mean_difference)`
(`r fmt(knn_ari$difference_ci_low)` to `r fmt(knn_ari$difference_ci_high)`),
with adjusted mutual information higher by `r fmt(knn_ami$mean_difference)`.
The spectral embedding is deterministic, so the hypergraph variants vary
little between seeds and the intervals reflect the seed variance of UMAP in
BERTopic. Only the cluster assignments are scored; the topic
representations of BERTopic are not compared.

## Choice of method

Label spreading with `normalization = "class_mass"` suits corpora whose
classes are roughly balanced or whose labels are few. The argmax without
normalization assigns most documents to the largest class when the seeds are
unbalanced. The random-walk Laplacian (`type = "random_walk"`) uses the
tf-idf weights in the walk and was the most accurate hypergraph method on
Ohsumed. On corpora with many unbalanced classes, a tf-idf centroid is a
strong baseline at almost no cost, and the published HyperGAT holds the
highest accuracy reported for these corpora.
